dct_description_sm: Climate change in the Arctic has the potential to affect mercury concentrations ([Hg]) in freshwater fishes. Land-use changes as a result of development can further influence mercury inputs to lakes. Mercury can accumulate in apex-predator fish muscle to concentrations exceeding those considered safe for subsistence consumption by humans. Fish species such as Lake trout are typical apex-predators of Arctic lakes and can be a significant source of food for local indigenous peoples. The influence of abiotic factors, which are climate influenced, and biological parameters on Hg accumulation in apex-predators are not well understood. The Husky Lakes complex, located between Tuk and Inuvik, is the dominant landscape feature along the proposed routes of the all-weather road to connect these two communities. It is currently utilized by members of both communities for hunting and fishing. This multiyear investigation combines aspects of climate change effects on lakes and resources with land use changes (road construction, cabin developments, and more convenient year round access to the lakes by community members). Monitoring effects thereof should occur prior to, during and after the construction of the proposed all-weather road. Local people of Inuvik and especially Tuk utilize the Husky Lakes extensively for subsistence hunts and consumption. Many families from Tuk spend the spring on the lakes to collect fish for subsistence consumption (jigging through the ice), while some families use nets under the ice in the fall to, in part, collect food for their dogs. Mercury concentrations in fish from these lakes that are commonly used for subsistence fishing by community members are mostly unknown.
dct_title_s: Mercury concentrations and biological information on the Husky Lakes, Northwest Territories
